bib.title: Principled Instructions Are All You Need for Questioning LLaMA-1/2, GPT-3.5/4

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Principled Instructions Are All You Need for Questioning LLaMA-1/2, GPT-3.5/4", Sondos Mahmoud Bsharat, Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen (VILA Lab, MBZUAI). arXiv:2312.16171v2, 18 Jan 2024 (preprint), 2023.

COVERAGE: all 26 pages, 73000 chars; main text, tables, figure text, limitations and references were all read. Figures 4-12 are charts, so only their axis text and heatmap numbers were extracted. No appendix beyond Figs 10-16. The extraction is fine, not scanned. No embedded instructions found.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The paper proposes 26 prompt principles in five categories: Prompt Structure and Clarity, Specificity and Information, User Interaction and Engagement, Content and Language Style, Complex Tasks and Coding. Table 1 is "randomly ordered".
  number: 26 principles
  quote: "we group them into five categories as in Table 2: (1) Prompt Structure and Clarity"
  where: p.4-6 (Tables 1-2)
- Headline gain, GPT-4 only: principled prompts raised quality by 57.7% and accuracy by 36.4% on average.
  number: 57.7% / 36.4%
  setup: manually built ATLAS benchmark, GPT-4, human evaluation, one response per question
  quote: "enhanced both the quality and accuracy of the LLM responses by an average of 57.7% and 36.4%, respectively, when applied to GPT-4"
  where: p.3
- Gains grow with model size.
  number: ">20%" for LLaMA-2-7B to GPT-4
  quote: "the performance gains when moving from LLaMA-2-7B to GPT-4 exceed 20%"
  where: p.3
  Relative correctness: "applying the principles generally leads to a performance increase of over 10% across different models on average. For larger models, this enhancement can surpass 20%." (p.10-11). Also "the larger the model, the greater the increase in correctness improvement" (p.11).
- Boosting averages about 50% across models.
  number: ~50%
  quote: "On average, there is a stable 50% improvement across different LLMs."
  where: p.10
- Absolute correctness is low.
  number: 20-40% average; large models above 40%
  quote: "these models achieve 20%∼40% accuracy on the averaged performance"; "for large models, the accuracy can reach more than 40%"
  where: p.9
  Fig 11 heatmap, absolute correctness per model: GPT-4 values run 45-85% (for example 80 for principles 2 and 12 and 85 for principles 24 and 26). Rows are principles 1-13, 16-20, 24-26; columns run LLaMA-1-7B to GPT-4, in the figure's column order. LLaMA-1-7B values are 5-25%.
- Boosting heatmap (Fig 10): principle 14 (ask the user questions) scores 100% on every model.
  quote: "for principle 14, as shown in Fig. 4, it has improved all questions it is applied to."
  where: p.9
  Principle 14 is not included in the correctness tests. The highest GPT-4 boosts are 100% for principles 2, 5 (as I read the heatmap), 25 and 26. The row-to-principle mapping is my reading of the unlabeled heatmap, so treat the individual cells with caution.
- Larger models gain most from principles 2 (audience), 5 (explain simply), 15, 16 (role), 25 and 26.
  quote: "In the cases of principles 2, 5, 15, 16, 25 and 26, the large-scale models get the most improvement"
  where: p.9
- Relative correctness gains (Fig 12, GPT-4): up to 55% for principle 7 (few-shot). Its row is 25 25 20 35 30 30 55.
  Principle 7 is the largest in most columns. The 7B models gain 0-25%.
  where: p.14
- Principle list items relevant to the note (verbatim from Table 1):
  - P1: "no need to be polite with LLM so there is no need to add phrases like "please", "if you don't mind", "thank you""
  - P4: "Employ affirmative directives such as 'do,' while steering clear of negative language like 'don't'"
  - P6: "Add "I'm going to tip $xxx for a better solution!""
  - P8: "start with '###Instruction###', followed by either '###Example###' or '###Question###'... Use one or more line breaks to separate instructions, examples, questions, context, and input data"
  - P9: "Your task is" and "You MUST"
  - P10: "You will be penalized"
  - P12: "think step by step"
  - P16: "Assign a role to the large language models"
  - P17: "Use Delimiters"
  - P20: "Use output primers"
  - P7/P19: few-shot and CoT combined with few-shot.
  where: p.5
- Design principles listed: conciseness and clarity, contextual relevance, task alignment, example demonstrations, avoiding bias, incremental prompting.
  quote: "overly verbose or ambiguous prompts can confuse the model or lead to irrelevant responses"
  where: p.7
- The paper offers no per-principle ablation of politeness, tipping or penalty. Fig 1 shows only anecdotes. In the tip example the GPT-4 answer to the logic question is longer and more structured, but it reaches the same conclusion.

SETUP (exact)
- Benchmark: ATLAS [19], "manually crafted". Standard subset across domains, plus a challenging subset for reasoning.
  quote: "For each principle and the challenging subset, it contains 20 human-selected questions with and without the principled prompts."
  where: p.7
  So there are 20 questions per principle and each result is a multiple of 5%.
- One response per question: "we utilize a single response for each question."
- Scoring: human evaluation of paired responses with and without the principle, "Similar to [10, 26]" (AlpacaEval, MT-Bench). The number and identity of the raters, the rubric and the agreement are not reported.
- Models: instruction-finetuned LLaMA-1-{7,13}, LLaMA-2-{7,13}, off-the-shelf LLaMA-2-70B-chat, GPT-3.5 (ChatGPT) and GPT-4. Scale groups: small = 7B, medium = 13B, large = 70B and GPT-3.5/4.
- Boosting: "the percentage increase in response quality across a set of questions when the proposed principles are applied", on simpler tasks. Correctness: absolute and relative accuracy on complex reasoning tasks. Principles 14, 15, 21, 22 and 23 are excluded from correctness. The correctness figures cover principles 1-13, 16-20 and 24-26.
- The paper does not state the sampling temperature, whether the prompts were manually rewritten for each principle, or the exact baseline wording.

LIMITS
- Authors concede (p.19): "the effectiveness of these principles may diminish when dealing with questions that are very complex or highly specialized"; other architectures "might respond in different ways"; "our assessment of improvement and correctness percentages was based on a limited selection of questions"; and "the criteria and results may vary across various personnel assessments".
- My reading, not the authors': there is no statistical test or confidence interval. At n=20 per cell, one question is 5 points. Human judges were unblinded as far as is stated. Boosting is subjective quality, not a task metric. The "improvement" is a win rate over the baseline rather than a score difference, and the paper does not clearly define the percentage. There are no public benchmarks such as MMLU or GSM8K. The CoT principle was tested on the LLaMA-2-13B derivative example, and the paper's own example answer is still wrong. The 57.7% figure looks like a headline GPT-4 average and is not shown by any figure I could read. Only the 2023-era models are covered, with no reasoning models. The tipping and threat principles were reported as combined results with no standalone effect or harm analysis. The conclusion says "constrained shot prompting" was used.
- Dated: the models are GPT-4 from 2023 and LLaMA-1/2. Later work found politeness, tipping and threat effects to be inconsistent. I cannot cite that from this source.

BUILDS ON (as printed): Brown et al. 2020 (GPT-3 few-shot); Wei et al. 2023 (chain-of-thought); Zhou et al. 2023 (least-to-most); Arora et al. 2022 (Ask Me Anything); Li et al. 2023 (directional stimulus prompting); White et al. 2023 (prompt pattern catalog, the source for principle 15, [16] in Table 2, and the origin of the "ask me questions" pattern); Lampinen et al. 2022 (explanations in context); Li et al. 2023 AlpacaEval and Zheng et al. 2023 MT-Bench (paired evaluation). ATLAS is cited as [19].

CODE: none. The only template-like items are the delimiter and format principle (P8, p.5): "###Instruction###" / "###Example###" / "###Question###", and the P14 phrase "From now on, I would like you to ask me questions to ...".

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): before and after for P5 and P6; the tip and "explain to a 5-year-old" examples.
- Fig 2 (p.8): P13 unbiased wording.
- Fig 3 (p.9): P7 few-shot fixes a "helpful or not" label.
- Fig 4 (p.10): average boosting per principle by scale.
- Fig 5 (p.10): absolute correctness per principle by scale.
- Fig 6 (p.11): relative correctness improvement per principle by scale.
- Fig 7-9 (p.12-13): the same three metrics per model.
- Fig 10-12 (p.13-14): per-principle by per-model heatmaps. These give the most data.
- Fig 13-16 (p.15-18): LLaMA-2-7B/13B examples; P12 and the "Explanation:" primer.

PROBLEMS: Charts are not machine-readable, so values come from heatmap text only. The row labels in the heatmaps are not extracted and are inferred from the principle order. The heatmap columns follow the figure's x-axis order. The Fig 13 example shows the principled prompt with an apparent typo ("Advce", "wrk") in Fig 3. The prompt text in Fig 14 is garbled by extraction. No embedded instructions.
